name: Design a Real-Time Fraud Detection System
intent: Decide within about a hundred milliseconds whether a card payment is allowed, challenged or blocked, using fresh behaviour counters, rules and a model, and keep improving from the chargebacks that arrive weeks later.
codeTitle: velocity counters, scoring and a shadow rule
finalIntro: One card payment being scored, and a new rule being tested without any effect on customers.
prompt: Design the fraud detection for a payments platform that handles 5,000 card payments per second at the peak. Every payment must get a decision before the customer sees a result: allow, challenge with an extra check, or block. About 1 payment in 1,000 is fraud. Fraud analysts want to add new rules often, and the system must learn from chargebacks, which arrive 30 to 120 days after the payment.
functional: Score every payment and return allow, challenge or block
Use recent behaviour, such as how many payments a card, device or address made in the last minute or hour
Combine hand-written rules with a machine-learning model
Send a challenge, such as a one-time code or 3-D Secure, for the uncertain middle
Learn from chargebacks and analyst verdicts
Let analysts add and test new rules safely
nonFunctional: A decision within 100 ms at the 99th percentile, including all lookups
Handle 5,000 payments per second at the peak, with bursts to several times that during an attack
Counters reflect a payment within about a second
Few false positives, because blocking a good customer costs far more than a challenge
Keep working, with a safe default, when a dependency is slow or down
Every decision can be explained and replayed later for disputes and audits

firstAttempt.text: The payment service runs a few SQL queries before it charges the card: count this card's payments in the last hour, sum the amounts, check the address against a table. If a hard-coded threshold is passed, the payment is declined. Rules are changed by editing code and deploying it.
limits: Counting recent payments with a query on the main database is slow, and it competes with the payments themselves at the peak
Hard-coded rules can only say yes or no, so a good customer who trips one is simply declined
Nothing learns, because chargebacks that arrive weeks later never come back to the rules
A new rule goes straight to production, so a mistake declines real customers before anyone notices
If the database is slow, every payment is slow, and there is no plan for what to do when the check cannot finish

nodes.label: SQL checks in the payment service

steps.title: Compute velocity counters from a stream
steps.problem: The strongest fraud signals are about recent behaviour, such as five payments on one card in a minute, and asking the main database to count them for every payment is too slow and too heavy.
steps.fix: Every payment is published to an event stream, partitioned by card, and a stream processor keeps counters for each card, device, address and merchant: payments and total amount over the last minute, hour and day. Each window is kept as small time buckets (for example six buckets of ten seconds for a minute), so the oldest bucket simply expires and nothing is rescanned. The counters live in a fast key-value store that the Payment API reads with one lookup. The same key is always handled by the same partition, so a card's events are counted in order.
steps.tradeoff: A lookup takes a millisecond or two and does not touch the payments database. The counters are a moment behind, so two payments in the same instant may not see each other, and the memory grows with the number of distinct cards, devices and addresses.

steps.title: Score with rules and a model inside a latency budget
steps.problem: A pile of if statements cannot weigh many weak signals together, and a model alone is hard to explain and cannot react to a new attack on the same day.
steps.fix: A scoring service runs two things on the same features. Rules are exact and explainable, such as 'three or more payments in a minute adds 40 points', and analysts can change them without a deploy. A model, such as gradient-boosted trees, adds a graded score from dozens of features and is small enough to evaluate in a few milliseconds. The whole call has a deadline of about 100 ms, split into a budget: roughly 10 ms for the feature lookups, 5 ms for rules, 20 ms for the model and the rest for the network. Lookups are issued in parallel, and each one has its own timeout.
steps.tradeoff: The decision uses both precise knowledge from people and patterns learned from data. Every extra feature costs a lookup, so each one must earn its place, and the budget has to be watched as a metric or it creeps upward until the 99th percentile fails.

steps.title: Turn the score into allow, challenge or block
steps.problem: A yes or no is too blunt, because declining a good customer costs more than most frauds do, and most payments with a medium risk are in fact fine.
steps.fix: The score maps to three outcomes with two thresholds, for example under 40 allow, 40 to 69 challenge and 70 or more block. A challenge asks for something a thief rarely has, such as a one-time code or a 3-D Secure confirmation, so it removes most fraud while most honest customers pass. The thresholds are not guesses: they are chosen to minimise the expected cost, using the average loss for a missed fraud, the cost of a lost sale and the friction cost of a challenge, and they differ by amount and by merchant type. Every decision is stored with its features and rule versions so it can be replayed.
steps.tradeoff: The middle band recovers sales that a hard block would lose. A challenge adds friction and some customers abandon, and a stored decision log is large and holds personal data that needs access control and a retention limit.

steps.title: Close the loop with chargebacks
steps.problem: A chargeback is the truth about a payment, but it arrives 30 to 120 days later, and until the model sees it nothing improves.
steps.fix: Chargebacks and analyst verdicts are joined to the stored decision record by payment id, and the features that were used at that moment are kept, not recomputed, so training sees exactly what the scorer saw. Labels are marked with their age: a payment from last week with no chargeback is not yet known to be good, so recent weeks are given a lower weight or left out. The model is retrained on a schedule, evaluated against a held-out recent period, and only then offered for release. Challenges produce early labels as well, because a failed challenge is strong evidence.
steps.tradeoff: The system adapts to new fraud patterns without anyone writing a rule. The labels are late and biased, since blocked payments never produce a chargeback, so the model cannot learn from what it prevented unless a small random share is allowed through for measurement.

steps.title: Roll out every new rule in shadow mode first
steps.problem: A rule that looks sharp on a few examples can decline thousands of good customers an hour, and by the time the complaints arrive the damage is done.
steps.fix: A new rule, or a new model version, first runs in shadow mode: the scorer evaluates it on live traffic, records what it would have decided next to the real decision, and acts on nothing. A report compares the two: how many decisions would change, how many of those payments later turned out to be fraud, and how many would have been good customers. When the numbers justify it, the rule moves to a small share of traffic, then to everyone, behind a flag with a kill switch, and it is watched against the false positive rate.
steps.tradeoff: A bad rule is found before it costs money, and every rule has evidence behind it. The evidence for fraud is slow because chargebacks are late, so shadow mode uses early labels and review verdicts first, and it needs the extra compute for evaluating rules that do not act.

steps.title: Fail safe, and send the doubtful cases to people
steps.problem: Counters, the model or the whole scorer can be slow or down exactly when an attack makes traffic spike, and the payment still needs an answer.
steps.fix: Every dependency has a fallback. If a counter lookup times out, its feature takes a neutral default and the rules that do not need it still run. If the scorer misses its deadline, a very simple local rule set decides: low amounts are allowed, high amounts are challenged. Under extreme load the system sheds the least valuable work first, such as shadow evaluation. Cases in a narrow grey zone, and large payments, go to a review queue where analysts decide within minutes, and their verdicts are early labels for the training data.
steps.tradeoff: Payments keep flowing and the worst case is bounded and known. A fallback is less accurate than the full path, so how often it fires is an alarm in itself, and analysts are a limited and expensive resource that only a small share of payments can use.

failures.scenario: The counter store is unavailable or very slow
failures.impact: The scorer has no recent behaviour, so a burst of stolen-card payments looks like ordinary traffic, or every payment waits for the timeout.
failures.answer: Each lookup has a short timeout and a circuit breaker, so a failing store is skipped quickly instead of delaying every payment. Missing features take a neutral value, the scorer keeps the rules that do not need them, and a stricter threshold applies for larger amounts while the degraded mode lasts. The fraction of decisions made in this mode is alerted on, and a replica or the other region takes over the counters.

failures.scenario: A card-testing attack sends 100,000 small payments a minute
failures.impact: The attacker is checking which stolen card numbers are valid, and the load can push the scorer past its deadline for everybody.
failures.answer: Velocity counters keyed by device, IP address and merchant catch the pattern even though each card is used only once. A rate limit and a block rule act early, before the expensive model runs, and the system sheds shadow work and low-value checks first. The attack's features are written to a deny list that is shared by all instances.

failures.scenario: A new rule declines good customers
failures.impact: False positives rise, sales fall and support calls start, and a deploy is the only way to turn the rule off.
failures.answer: The rule was run in shadow mode first, and the report showed how many good payments it would have touched, so it started with a small share of traffic. It is controlled by a flag, so the kill switch removes it in seconds without a deploy, and an alert on the decline rate by rule pages the on-call analyst.

failures.scenario: Events arrive late, twice or out of order
failures.impact: A counter is too low and lets a burst through, or too high and challenges a good customer.
failures.answer: Each event has a unique payment id and the processor ignores one it has already counted, so a replay does not inflate a counter. Buckets are keyed by event time, and a late event within a short allowed lateness is added to the right bucket, while a very late one is dropped from the counters and kept in the log for training. The decision log records which counter values were used.

failures.scenario: Fraudsters change their behaviour after the model is trained
failures.impact: Detection quality falls slowly, because the model learned last quarter's patterns and the labels for the new pattern have not arrived yet.
failures.answer: Monitoring compares the score distribution and the share of challenged payments with the last weeks, and alerts on a shift before chargebacks confirm it. Analysts add a rule for the new pattern the same day, tested in shadow mode, and the model is retrained as early labels from failed challenges and reviews come in.

alternatives.title: How features are computed

options.name: On demand with a query
options.pro: Always exact and no extra system
options.con: Slow at the peak and it loads the main database

options.name: Streaming counters in a key-value store
options.pro: One fast lookup and a fresh value within a second
options.con: Another pipeline to run, and the counters can be slightly behind

options.name: Nightly batch features
options.pro: Cheap and easy to compute over a long history
options.con: Too stale for burst attacks, so use it only for slow features such as a customer's usual spend

alternatives.pick: Streaming counters for recent windows, with batch features for long-term history.

alternatives.title: Rules or a model

options.name: Rules only
options.con: They cannot weigh many weak signals, and they grow into a tangle

options.name: Model only
options.pro: Finds patterns that nobody wrote down
options.con: Slow to react to a new attack, and harder to explain to a customer or a regulator

options.name: Both, the rules on top of the model
options.pro: Fast reaction from rules and subtle detection from the model
options.con: Two things to maintain and test

alternatives.pick: Both: rules for what is known and urgent, a model for the rest.

alternatives.title: What to do when the check cannot finish

options.name: Fail open and allow
options.pro: No lost sales and no friction
options.con: An attacker who can slow the system gets free passes

options.name: Fail closed and decline
options.pro: No fraud loss during the outage
options.con: Every customer is declined, which is a worse outage than the fraud

options.name: A simple fallback by risk
options.pro: Small amounts pass and large amounts are challenged, so the loss is bounded
options.con: It needs a second, simpler decision path that is tested regularly

alternatives.pick: A simple fallback by amount and risk, with an alert as soon as it is used.

alternatives.title: How to choose thresholds

options.name: A fixed score everywhere
options.con: A 50 point score means different things for a 5 dollar and a 5,000 dollar payment

options.name: A cost-based threshold per segment
options.pro: Blocks where the expected loss is higher than the cost of a lost sale
options.con: Needs good estimates of loss, abandonment and friction, and regular review

alternatives.pick: Cost-based thresholds by amount band, reviewed each month.

quiz.question: The payment service runs three SQL count queries on the main database before every charge, such as 'payments by this card in the last hour'. At 5,000 payments per second the database is slow and the payments themselves suffer. What is the best fix?
options: Add an index and a read replica for the count queries, so they stop competing with the payment writes and each one reads far fewer rows.
Publish payments to a stream and keep bucketed counters per card, device and address in a key-value store, read with one lookup.
Cache each card's query result for five minutes, so repeated payments by the same card skip the database.
Compute the counts in a nightly batch job and look them up at scoring time.
quiz.explanation: Counters kept as small time buckets expire the oldest bucket instead of rescanning, and they stay fresh within a second. A replica still scans rows per payment, and a five-minute cache lets a burst of fraud through. Nightly features are far too old for burst attacks.

quiz.question: A payment has a risk score that means about a 2% chance of fraud. Assume a challenge costs about $1 in lost sales and stops most fraud, a lost good sale costs about $60 of margin on the large payment, and a fraud costs the full amount. What is the best treatment of a $15 payment and of a $2,000 payment?
options: Allow both, since 98% of payments at this score are good, so the same treatment is fine for any amount and any merchant.
Challenge both, since a single fixed threshold is easy to explain and a challenge is cheap compared with a fraud loss.
Allow the $15 payment (expected fraud loss about $0.30) and challenge the $2,000 payment (expected loss about $40, and a block loses a good sale 98% of the time).
Allow the $15 payment and block the $2,000 payment, since the $40 expected loss is far above the $1 friction cost.
quiz.explanation: Thresholds are chosen by expected cost per amount band. At $15 even a challenge costs more than the fraud risk, while at $2,000 the risk justifies friction. Blocking is worse than allowing here because it loses a good sale 98% of the time, so the challenge is the cheaper middle.

quiz.question: An attacker tests 100,000 distinct stolen card numbers a minute with $1 payments, each card used once, through 50 devices and one merchant. Per-card counters show a single payment for every card. What catches this attack?
options: Velocity counters keyed by device, IP and merchant, with a rate limit before the model.
Lower the per-card threshold to one payment per hour, so any second use of a card triggers a block.
Retrain the model on the new chargebacks, so it learns the attack pattern from labelled examples.
Send every small payment to the analyst review queue, where people decide within minutes and their verdicts become labels for training.
quiz.explanation: Each card appears once, so only counters on the shared entities, the 50 devices and the merchant, reveal the pattern, and cheap rules act before the costly model. A per-card limit never fires, chargebacks arrive 30 to 120 days later, and 100,000 payments a minute is far beyond what analysts can review.
